lines.text: Technology and gadgets have become inseparable from modern British life — shaping how people work, communicate, shop, travel, and entertain themselves. The smartphone is the dominant device: over 90% of British adults own one, using it for an average of four hours daily. Beyond calls and messaging, smartphones serve as cameras, wallets (contactless payment via Apple Pay or Google Pay), navigation tools, fitness trackers, and entertainment centres. Laptops and tablets remain essential for work and education, though the boundary between 'work device' and 'personal device' has blurred with remote working. Smart home technology is growing rapidly: voice assistants (Amazon Alexa, Google Home), smart thermostats (Nest, Hive), smart doorbells (Ring), and automated lighting systems are increasingly common in British homes. Wearable technology — smartwatches, fitness bands, and wireless earbuds — has moved from novelty to necessity. The Apple Watch alone outsells the entire Swiss watch industry. E-readers (Kindle) have transformed reading habits, though physical books remain surprisingly resilient. Streaming services (Netflix, Disney+, BBC iPlayer) have replaced traditional television viewing for many, while gaming — from console (PlayStation, Xbox) to mobile — is the UK's largest entertainment industry, surpassing film and music combined. The UK's tech sector is Europe's largest, contributing over £150 billion annually to the economy and employing nearly two million people.

lines.text: 'Dead' or 'flat' (British) — not 'empty'. 'My phone's dead', 'the battery's flat', 'it's on 2%', 'I'm running low on battery'. 'Empty' is for containers (empty glass, empty room).
lines.name: 'Dead' or 'flat' (British) — not 'empty'. 'My phone's dead', 'the battery's flat', 'it's on 2%', 'I'm running low on battery'. 'Empty' is for containers (empty glass, empty room).

lines.text: ✓  "Can you lend me your charger?" / "Can I borrow your charger?"
lines.name: ✓ "Can you lend me your charger?" / "Can I borrow your charger?"

lines.text: 'Lend' (give temporarily) vs 'borrow' (take temporarily). 'Can you LEND me...?' or 'Can I BORROW...?' Never 'borrow me' — that confuses the direction of the exchange.

lines.text: 'App' is standard — 'application' is technically correct but sounds overly formal in everyday conversation. 'Download an app', 'install an app', 'update the app', 'delete the app'.

lines.text: 'Working' not 'functioning' in everyday British English. 'Playing up' (British) = malfunctioning intermittently. 'The Wi-Fi keeps dropping', 'the connection is patchy', 'the signal is weak'.
